summary.text: Take the composite number \(N=23492890653051=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\), a product of five distinct primes. The gcd-sum is multiplicative and equals \(2p-1\) at a prime, so at \(N\) it is \(610815156979325\), and \(1+610815156979325=26N\); hence the relevant gcd is \(N\) and the resulting value is \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n),
\qquad
 a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+A(n))}.
\]
We will exhibit a composite positive integer \(N\) for which \(a(N)=1\).

The counterexample is
\[
N=23492890653051
  =3\cdot 37\cdot 43\cdot 42307\cdot 116341.
\]
The proof has three parts: first, a formula for the gcd sum \(A(n)\); second, verification that the five displayed factors are distinct primes; and third, the numerical evaluation of \(A(N)\).

### 1. The gcd-sum formula

Write \(\varphi(m)\) for Euler's totient function. For every positive integer \(n\),
\[
A(n)=\sum_{d\mid n} d\,\varphi(n/d). \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, partition the integers \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) according to the value
\(d=\gcd(k,n)\). Such a value \(d\) must divide \(n\). If \(d\mid n\), then
\(\gcd(k,n)=d\) holds exactly when \(k=dj\), where
\[
1\leq j\leq n/d
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd(j,n/d)=1.
\]
There are \(\varphi(n/d)\) such integers \(j\), and every one of the corresponding terms \(\gcd(k,n)\) contributes \(d\). Summing over all divisors \(d\) proves (1).

Define
\[
G(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d).
\]
Thus (1) says that \(A(n)=G(n)\).

The function \(G\) is multiplicative: if \(\gcd(m,n)=1\), then
\[
G(mn)=G(m)G(n). \tag{2}
\]
To see this directly, every divisor of \(mn\) has a unique form \(d_1d_2\), with
\(d_1\mid m\) and \(d_2\mid n\). Moreover,
\[
\frac{mn}{d_1d_2}=\frac m{d_1}\frac n{d_2},
\]
and these last two factors are coprime. Euler's totient is multiplicative on coprime arguments (this follows, for example, by identifying reduced residue classes modulo a product via the Chinese remainder theorem). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(mn)
 &=\sum_{d_1\mid m}\sum_{d_2\mid n}
 d_1d_2\,
 \varphi\!\left(\frac m{d_1}\frac n{d_2}\right)\\
 &=\sum_{d_1\mid m}\sum_{d_2\mid n}
 \left(d_1\varphi(m/d_1)\right)
 \left(d_2\varphi(n/d_2)\right)\\
 &=G(m)G(n),
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (2).

If \(p\) is prime, its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\). Consequently,
\[
G(p)=\varphi(p)+p\varphi(1)=(p-1)+p=2p-1. \tag{3}
\]
It follows from (2) and (3) that if \(n\) is a product of distinct primes \(p_i\), then
\[
A(n)=G(n)=\prod_i(2p_i-1). \tag{4}
\]

### 2. Primality of the factors

The numbers \(3,37,43\) are prime by immediate trial division: neither \(37\) nor \(43\) is divisible by any prime at most its square root, namely \(2,3,5\).

For completeness, we also give explicit primality certificates for \(42307\) and \(116341\). We use the following elementary form of Pocklington's criterion.

Suppose \(M>1\), and let \(F\) be a squarefree product of known primes such that
\[
F\mid M-1 \quad\text{and}\quad F>\sqrt M.
\]
Suppose that for every prime \(q\mid F\) there is an integer \(b\) satisfying
\[
b^{M-1}\equiv1\pmod M
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd\bigl(b^{(M-1)/q}-1,M\bigr)=1. \tag{5}
\]
Then \(M\) is prime. Here is the proof. Let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(M\). The first congruence in (5) says that the multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(r\) divides \(M-1\). The gcd condition says that this order does not divide \((M-1)/q\), so \(q\) divides the order. Since the order modulo \(r\) divides \(r-1\), every prime \(q\mid F\) divides \(r-1\). As \(F\) is squarefree, this gives \(F\mid r-1\), and hence
\(r\geq F+1>\sqrt M\). But every composite integer has a prime divisor at most its square root. Thus \(M\) cannot be composite.

First consider \(M=42307\). We have
\[
42307-1=42306=66\cdot641.
\]
The integer \(641\) is prime. Indeed, \(25<\sqrt{641}<26\), and division by the primes at most \(25\) gives the following nonzero remainders:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
q&2&3&5&7&11&13&17&19&23\\ \hline
641\bmod q&1&2&1&4&3&4&12&14&20.
\end{array}
\]
Take \(F=641\), for which \(F^2=410881>42307\). Repeated squaring modulo \(42307\) gives
\[
2^{42306}\equiv1\pmod{42307},
\qquad
2^{66}\equiv2666\pmod{42307}.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\gcd(2666-1,42307)=\gcd(2665,42307)=1.
\]
For instance, the Euclidean algorithm ends with
\[
42307=15\cdot2665+2332,
\quad 2665=2332+333,
\quad 2332=7\cdot333+1.
\]
Thus criterion (5), with \(q=641\) and base \(b=2\), proves that \(42307\) is prime.

Now consider \(M=116341\). Its predecessor factors as
\[
116341-1=116340=4\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\]
The integer \(277\) is prime: \(16<\sqrt{277}<17\), and its remainders upon division by the primes at most \(16\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrr}
q&2&3&5&7&11&13\\ \hline
277\bmod q&1&1&2&4&2&4,
\end{array}
\]
all nonzero. Let
\[
F=3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277=29085.
\]
This is squarefree, divides \(116340\), and
\[
F^2=845937225>116341,
\]
so \(F>\sqrt{116341}\). Using the single base \(b=7\), repeated squaring modulo \(116341\) gives
\[
7^{116340}\equiv1\pmod{116341},
\]
and, for the four prime factors of \(F\),
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&(116340)/q&7^{116340/q}\bmod116341\\ \hline
3&38780&50801\\
5&23268&113165\\
7&16620&86734\\
277&420&49944.
\end{array}
\]
The corresponding gcds are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\gcd(50800,116341)&=1,\\
\gcd(113164,116341)&=1,\\
\gcd(86733,116341)&=1,\\
\gcd(49943,116341)&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are ordinary Euclidean-algorithm computations. Thus (5) applies for every prime divisor \(q\) of \(F\), and it proves that \(116341\) is prime.

Therefore all five numbers
\[
3,\ 37,\ 43,\ 42307,\ 116341
\]
are distinct primes. In particular they are pairwise coprime, so the multiplicative formula (4) applies to their product.

### 3. Evaluation at the counterexample

The successive products of the five prime factors are
\[
3\cdot37=111,
\qquad
111\cdot43=4773,
\]
\[
4773\cdot42307=201931311,
\qquad
201931311\cdot116341=23492890653051.
\]
Thus their product really is the claimed number \(N\).

For these primes, the factors \(2p-1\) appearing in (4) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
p&3&37&43&42307&116341\\ \hline
2p-1&5&73&85&84613&232681.
\end{array}
\]
Consequently,
\[
A(N)=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\]
The successive products are
\[
5\cdot73=365,
\qquad
365\cdot85=31025,
\]
\[
31025\cdot84613=2625118325,
\]
and
\[
2625118325\cdot232681=610815156979325.
\]
Hence
\[
A(N)=610815156979325.
\]
Adding one gives
\[
1+A(N)=610815156979326.
\]
A direct multiplication now yields
\[
26N
=26\cdot23492890653051
=610815156979326
=1+A(N). \tag{6}
\]
Thus \(N\mid 1+A(N)\). Since the gcd of a positive integer \(N\) with any multiple of \(N\) is \(N\), equation (6) gives
\[
\gcd(N,1+A(N))=N.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(N)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,1+A(N))}=\frac NN=1.
\]

Finally, \(N\neq1\), and \(N\) is not prime: it has the proper divisor \(3\), explicitly
\[
N=3\cdot7830963551017,
\]
with both factors greater than \(1\). We have therefore found a positive composite integer \(N\) satisfying \(a(N)=1\). This contradicts the proposed equivalence
\[
a(n)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(n=1\text{ or }n\text{ is prime}),
\]
and hence disproves the conjecture.
